intro: Vltava, the second part of Má vlast, follows the river from two spring streams through Bohemia to Prague, according to the programme that Smetana approved. He finished it on 8 December 1874, seven weeks after he lost his hearing.

cues.title: Opening: the two springs
cues.text: The programme begins with two spring streams, one warm and lively, the other cool and sluggish, that join to form the river. The score opens with two flutes marked solo over pizzicato strings. The clarinets join them in the running figures that follow.
cues.evidence: Programme approved by Smetana, printed in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), pp. 58–59. Eulenburg miniature score, pp. 1–4: two flutes marked Solo, pizzicato violins, then clarinets in the semiquaver figures. https://archive.org/details/mavlastvltavno20000unse
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Main theme in E minor
cues.text: At bar 40 the first violins, with the oboes, play the main theme in 6/8. It begins with an upbeat B, then E–F♯–G–A and a repeated B. The second violins, violas and cellos run in semiquavers marked sempre ondeggiante.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg miniature score, pp. 5–6, bars 39–42: the score prints bar numbers every tenth bar, and 40 stands above the bar where the theme begins in the first violins and oboes; the second violin, viola and cello parts carry the marking sempre ondeggiante. https://archive.org/details/mavlastvltavno20000unse
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition after deafness, 1874
cues.text: Smetana’s right ear had already failed when he lost the hearing in his left on the morning of 20 October 1874. He began Vltava on 20 November and finished it on 8 December.
cues.evidence: Smetana to J. Finch Thorne, 11 December 1881, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), pp. 47–49: right ear lost in October, left ear on the morning of 20 October 1874. Bedřich Smetana Museum catalogue, My Country: Vltava begun 20 November, finished 8 December 1874. https://bedrichsmetana.nm.cz/en/work/detail/my-country/133

cues.title: Forest hunt
cues.text: In the programme Smetana approved, the river flows through dark forest, where the horns sound a hunt.
cues.evidence: Programme approved by Smetana, printed in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 58: the river flows through the dark forest, “from which the merry hunt sounds in the tones of the horn”. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: Peasant wedding
cues.text: The programme next passes meadows where country people hold a wedding feast, with cheerful tunes and a round dance.
cues.evidence: Programme approved by Smetana, printed in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 58. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: First performance, Prague, 1875
cues.text: Vltava was first played on 4 April 1875 at the Žofín hall in Prague under Adolf Čech. The concert was Smetana’s own, given to pay for consultations with specialists about his hearing.
cues.evidence: Bedřich Smetana Museum catalogue, My Country (Smetana’s own list of 1875: first performed at his concert at Žofín on 4 April 1875 under Čech); Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), pp. 54–55, on the purpose of the concert. https://bedrichsmetana.nm.cz/en/work/detail/my-country/133

cues.title: Moonlight episode, the nymphs
cues.text: In the programme, nymphs dance in a ring at night over the silver surface of the river, and old castles look down in silence.
cues.evidence: Programme approved by Smetana, printed in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), pp. 58–59. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: St John’s Rapids
cues.text: In the programme, the river is hemmed in by rocks and hills and foams through a narrow valley, forming rapids and dangerous whirlpools.
cues.evidence: Programme approved by Smetana, printed in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 59: the rapids at St John. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: After the rapids
cues.text: After the rapids, the programme has the river flow in majestic breadth towards Prague.
cues.evidence: Programme approved by Smetana, printed in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 59. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: Letter to Adolf Čech, 1882
cues.text: After the first complete performance of Má vlast on 5 November 1882, Smetana wrote to the conductor Adolf Čech: “It was as if I had heard one piece after another, in spirit but almost in reality.”
cues.evidence: Smetana to Adolf Čech, November 1882, in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 90; the performance date from the Bedřich Smetana Museum catalogue. Translated from the German text. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

cues.title: Vyšehrad and the river’s end
cues.text: In the programme the river flows towards Prague, where the famous old Vyšehrad greets it from its rock, and then loses itself in the far distance.
cues.evidence: Programme approved by Smetana, printed in Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895), p. 59. https://archive.org/details/11658530bsb

composer.epithet: Czech composer and conductor from Litomyšl, whose operas for Prague’s Provisional Theatre include The Bartered Bride; deaf from 1874, he then wrote Má vlast and the quartet From My Life.
facts: Prague from 1843, with the blind teacher Josef Proksch; corresponded with Liszt from 1848 and visited him at Weimar in 1857

Music teacher to Count Thun, 1844–47 · own music institute, Prague, from 1848 · Harmoniska Sällskapet, Gothenburg, 1856–61 · opera of the Provisional Theatre, Prague, from 1866 until deafness ended his conducting in 1874
Letter to Liszt 1848 · Gothenburg 1856 · The Bartered Bride 1866 · deafness 1874 · Jabkenice 1875 · Má vlast complete 1882
Eight completed operas, the six symphonic poems of Má vlast, two string quartets, a piano trio, piano polkas and choruses

quote.text: I wanted to depict the course of my life in tones.
quote.source: Smetana to Josef Srb-Debrnov, 12 April 1878, on the String Quartet No. 1; translated from the German text printed in Bronislav Wellek, Friedrich Smetana (1895)

composer.background:
Bedřich Smetana was born on 2 March 1824 in the castle brewery at Litomyšl, where his father František was a master brewer. He was the first son after six daughters. At five he played first violin in a quartet on his father’s name day, and on 4 October 1830 he played the piano at an academy given for the emperor’s name day. He was schooled in German, at Jindřichův Hradec, Jihlava, Německý Brod, Prague and, from 1840, Plzeň. Because his schoolwork was suffering, his father put him there under the supervision of a cousin, Josef Franz Smetana, a gymnasium teacher.

In 1843 the cousin persuaded his father to send him to Prague to train as a musician. His parents had become poor and sent no money; the Kolář family took him in, and the blind composer Josef Proksch accepted him as a pupil. In 1844 he became music teacher to Count Leopold Thun, on the recommendation of Friedrich Kittl, director of the Conservatory, and until 1847 he spent much of each year at the Thun castles at Poběžovice and Nové Benátky.
